{{smaller block|''Voice'' as a scientific term may mean either the faculty of uttering audible sounds, or the body of audible sounds produced by the organs of respiration, especially the larynx of man and other animals: contradistinguished from ''speech'' or ''articulate language''. Voice is produced when air is driven by the muscles of expiration from the lungs through the trachea and strikes against the two vocal cords (see ''cord''<sup>1</sup>), the vibrations of which produce sounds varying in different animals according to the structure of the organs and the power which the animal possesses over them. Voice can, therefore, be found only in animals in which this system of respiration is developed, and the lungs and larynx (or syrinx) actually exist. Fishes, having no lungs, are dumb, as far as true vocal utterance is concerned, though various noises may issue from their throats (see ''croaker'', ''grunt'', and ''drum''). In man the superior organization and mobility of the tongue and lips, as well as the perfection of the larynx, enable him to modify his vocal sounds to an almost infinite extent. In ordinary speaking the tones of the voice have nearly all the same pitch, and the variety of the sounds is due rather to the action of the mouth-organs than to definite movements of the glottis and vocal cords. In singing the successive sounds correspond more or less closely to the ideal tones of the musical scale. The male voice admits of division into tenor and bass, and the female into soprano and contralto. The lowest female tone is an octave or so higher than the lowest tone of the male voice; and the female’s highest tone is about an octave above that of the male. The compass of both voices taken together is four octaves or more, the chief differences residing in the pitch and also in the timbre. In medicine, ''voice'' is the sound of utterance as transmitted through the lungs and chest-wall in auscultation. {{smaller block|Shall we give poor Buffière’s testimonial in mess-room dialect, in its native twanging ''vociferosity''?
{{right|''Carlyle'', Mirabeau.}}}}

'''vociferous''' (vọ̄-sif′e̤-rus), ''a.''   [< ''vocifer(ate)'' + ''-ous''.]   Making an outcry; clamorous; noisy: as, a ''vociferous'' partizan.
{{smaller block|Thrice-three ''vocif’rous'' heralds rose, to check the rout, and get
Ear to their Jove-kept governors. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, ii. 83.}}}}
{{smaller block|Flocks of ''vociferous'' geese cackled about the fields.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 161.}}}}
{{smaller block|Every mouth in the Netherlands became ''vociferous'' to denounce the hypocrisy by which a new act of condemnation had been promulgated under the name of a pardon.
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, II. 290.}}}}

'''vociferously''' (vọ̄-sif′e̤-rus-li), ''adv.'' In a vociferous manner; with great noise in calling or shouting.

'''vociferousness''' (vọ̄-sif′e̤-rus-nes), ''n.'' The character of being vociferous; clamorousness.

'''vocular''' (vok′ụ̄-lär), ''a.''   [< L. ''vocula'', a small or feeble voice (see ''vocule''), + ''-ar''<sup>3</sup>.]   Vocal. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He turned angrily round, and inquired what that young cur was howling for, and why Mr. Bumble did not favor him with something which would render the series of ''vocular'' exclamations so designated an involuntary process.
{{right|''Dickens'', Oliver Twist, vii.}}}}

'''vocule''' (vok′ūl), ''n.''   [< L. ''vocula'', a small or feeble voice, dim. of ''vox'' (''voc-''), voice: see ''voice''.]   A faint or slight sound of the voice, as that made by separating the organs in pronouncing ''p'', ''t'', or ''k''. [Rare.]

'''vodka''' (vōd′kä), ''n.''   [Russ. ''vodka'', brandy, dim. of ''voda'', water.]   A sort of whisky or brandy generally drunk in Russia, properly distilled from rye, but sometimes from potatoes.

{{smaller block|The captain shared with us his not very luxurious meal of dried Caspian carp and almost equally dry sausage, washed down by the never-failing glass of ''vodka'', and then we again started on our forward journey.
{{right|''O’Donovan'', Merv, iii.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Vodki'' is the chief means of intoxication.
{{right|''A. J. C. Hare'', Russia, i.}}}}

'''vodu''', ''a.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''voodoo.''

'''voe''' (vō), ''n.''   [Also ''vo'', Sc. ''vae''; < Icel. ''vágr'', also written ''vogr'', a creek, bay: common in local names.]   An inlet, bay, or creek. [Shetland.]

'''Voëtian''' (vō-ē′shian), ''n.''   [< ''Voëtius'' (see def.) + ''-an''.]   A follower of Voëtius of the Reformed Church in the Netherlands in the seventeenth century, who held, in opposition to Cocceius, to the literal sense in interpreting both the Old and the New Testament.

'''vogie''' (vō′gi), ''a.''   [Also ''voky, vokie''; origin obscure.]   Vain; proud; also, merry; cheery. [Scotch.]

<poem>We took a spring, and danced a fling.
And wow but we were ''vogie!''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Jacobite Relics'', p. 81. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}

'''voglite''' (vōg′līt), ''n.''   [Named after J. F. ''Vogl'', a German mineralogist.]   A hydrated carbonate of uranium, calcium, and copper, of an emerald-green color and pearly luster, occurring near Joachimsthal in Bohemia.

'''Vogt’s angle.''' In ''craniom.'', the angle formed by the junction of the nasobasilar and alveolonasal lines.

'''vogue''' (vōg), ''n.''   [< F. ''vogue'', fashion, vogue (= Sp. ''boga'', fashion, reputation, = Pg. It. ''voga'', a rowing), orig. sway, the swaying motion of a ship, the stroke of an oar, < ''voguer'' = Pr. Pg. ''vogar'' = Sp. ''bogar'' = It. ''vogare'', row or sail, proceed under sail, < OHG. ''wagōn'', MHG. ''wagen'', G. ''wogen'', fluctuate, float, < ''waga'', a waving, akin to ''wāg'', MHG. ''wāc'', a wave (> F. ''vague''), G. ''woge'', a wave: see ''waw''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The mode or fashion prevalent at any particular time; popular reception, repute, or estimation; common currency: now generally used in the phrase ''in vogue'': as, a particular style of dress was then ''in vogue''; a writer who was ''in vogue'' fifty years ago; such opinions are now ''in vogue''.
{{smaller block|The Lord Treasurer Weston is he who hath the greatest ''Vogue'' now at Court, but many great ones have clashed with him.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|Though Christianity were directly contrary to the Religions then ''in vogue'' in the world, yet they [men] knew of no other way of promoting it but by patience, humility, meekness, prayers for their persecutors, and tears when they saw them obstinate.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Wits of the Age, the great Beauties, and short-liv’d People of ''Vogue'', were always her Discourse and Imitation.
{{right|''Steele'', Tender Husband, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''vogue'' of operas holds up wonderfully, though we have had them a year.
{{right|''Swift'', Letter, March 22, 1708-9.}}}}
{{smaller block|I demanded who were the present theatrical writers ''in vogue''.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xviii.}}}}
'''2.''' General drift of ideas; rumor; report.

{{smaller block|The ''rogue'' of our few honest folks here is that Duck is absolutely to succeed Eusden in the laurel.
{{right|''Swift'', To Gay, Nov. 19, 1730.}}}}

{{smaller block|Some affirm the Earl of Suffolk . . . goes general of the fleet; but most opinions give it to my Lord Denbigh. . . . Captain Pennington hath the ''rogue'' to go his vice-admiral.
{{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', I. 131.}}}}

'''voice''' (vois), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''voyce''; < ME. ''voice'', ''woice'', earlier ''vois'', ''voys'', ''voiz'', ''voce'', < OF. ''vois'', ''voiz'', ''vuiz'', F. ''voix'' = Pr. ''votz'', ''voutz'' = Sp. Pg. ''voz'' = It. ''voce'', < L. ''vox'', a voice, utterance, cry, call, a speech, saying, sentence, maxim, word, language, = Gr. ἔπος (*Ϝέπος), a word (see ''epos'', ''epic''), = Skt. ''vachas'', speech. From the L. ''vox'', or the verb ''vocare'', call, are ult. E. ''vocal'', ''vowel'', ''vocable'', ''advocate'', ''advowson'', ''avocation'', ''vouch'', ''avouch'', ''convoke'', ''evoke'', ''invoke'', ''provoke'', ''revoke'', ''equivocal'', ''univocal'', ''vocation'', ''vociferate'', etc.]   '''1.''' The sound uttered by the mouths of living creatures; especially, human utterance in speaking, singing, crying, shouting, etc.; the sound made by a person in speaking, singing, crying, etc.; the character, quality, or expression of the sounds so uttered: as, to hear a ''voice''; to recognize a ''voice''; a loud ''voice''; a low ''voice''.

{{smaller block|Thei gon before him with processioun, with Cros and Holy Watre; and thei syngen Veni Creator Spiritus with an highe ''Voys'', and gon towardes him.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 244.}}}}

<poem>Ther sat a faucon over hire hed ful hye,
That with a pitous ''voys'' so gan to cry.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire’s Tale, l. 404.}}}}

<poem>Her ''voice'' was ever soft,
Gentle, and low, an excellent thing in woman.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, v. 3. 273.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Voice'' as a scientific term may mean either the faculty of uttering audible sounds, or the body of audible sounds produced by the organs of respiration, especially the larynx of man and other animals: contradistinguished from ''speech'' or ''articulate language''. Voice is produced when air is driven by the muscles of expiration from the lungs through the trachea and strikes against the two vocal cords (see ''cord''<sup>1</sup>), the vibrations of which produce sounds varying in different animals according to the structure of the organs and the power which the animal possesses over them. Voice can, therefore, be found only in animals in which this system of respiration is developed, and the lungs and larynx (or syrinx) actually exist. Fishes, having no lungs, are dumb, as far as true vocal utterance is concerned, though various noises may issue from their throats (see ''croaker'', ''grunt'', and ''drum''). In man the superior organization and mobility of the tongue and lips, as well as the perfection of the larynx, enable him to modify his vocal sounds to an almost infinite extent. In ordinary speaking the tones of the voice have nearly all the same pitch, and the variety of the sounds is due rather to the action of the mouth-organs than to definite movements of the glottis and vocal cords. In singing the successive sounds correspond more or less closely to the ideal tones of the musical scale. The male voice admits of division into tenor and bass, and the female into soprano and contralto. The lowest female tone is an octave or so higher than the lowest tone of the male voice; and the female’s highest tone is about an octave above that of the male. The compass of both voices taken together is four octaves or more, the chief differences residing in the pitch and also in the timbre. In medicine, ''voice'' is the sound of utterance as transmitted through the lungs and chest-wall in auscultation. In zoology, ''voice'' is ordinarily restricted to respiratory sounds or vocal utterance, as above explained, and as distinguished from any mechanical noise, like stridulation, etc. The more usual word for the voice of any animal is ''cry''; and the various cries, distinctive or characteristic of certain animals, take many distinctive terms, according to their vocal quality, as ''bark, bay, bellow, bleat, bray, cackle, call, caw, chatter, chirp, chirrup, cluck, coo, croak, crow, gabble, gobble, growl, grunt, hiss, honk, hoot, howl, low, mew, neigh, peep, pipe, purr, quack, roar, scream, screech, snarl, snort, song, squall, squawk, squeak, squeal, trumpet, twitter, warble, waul, whine, whinny, whistle, whoop, yawp, yell, yelp,'' and many others. The voices of some animals, as certain monkeys and large carnivores and ruminants, may be heard a mile or more. The voice reaches its highest development, in animals other than human, in the distinctively musical class of birds, some of which, notably parrots and certain corvine and sturnoid birds, can be taught to talk intelligible speech.}}

'''2.''' The faculty of speaking; speech; utterance.
{{smaller block|<poem>It [emancipation] shall bid the sad rejoice,
It shall give the dumb a ''voice,''
It shall belt with joy the earth !</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Laus Deo !}}}}

'''3.''' A sound produced by an inanimate object and regarded as representing the voice of an intelligent being: as, the ''voice'' of the winds.
{{smaller block|The floods have lifted up their ''voice.'' {{right|Ps. xciii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The twilight ''voice'' of distant bells.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Merrimack.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Rain was in the wind’s ''voice'' as it swept
Along the hedges where the lone quail crept.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 393.}}}}

'''4.''' Anything analogous to human speech which conveys impressions to any of the senses or to the mind.
{{smaller block|<poem>I, now the ''voice'' of the recorded law,
Pronounce a sentence on your brother’s life.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., ii. 4. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>E’en from the tomb the ''voice'' of Nature cries.</poem>
{{right|''Gray'', Elegy.}}}}

'''5.''' Opinion or choice expressed; the right of expressing an opinion; vote; suffrage: as, you have no ''voice'' in the matter.

<poem>''Sic.'' How now, my masters! have you chose this man?
''First Cit.'' He has our ''voices'', sir.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3. 164.}}

{{smaller block|Matters of moment were to be examined by a Iury, but determined by the maior part of the Councell, in which the President had two ''voyces.''
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 151.}}}}

{{smaller block|They who seek nothing but thir own just Liberty have always right to win it, and keep it, whenever they have Power, be the ''Voices'' never so numerous that oppose it.
{{right|''Milton'', Free Commonwealth.}}}}

{{smaller block|Let us call on God in the ''voice'' of the church.
{{right|''Bp. Fell.''}}}}

<poem>My ''voice'' is still for war.
Gods! can a Roman senate long debate
Which of the two to choose, slavery or death!</poem>{{right|''Addison'', Cato, ii. 1.}}

{{smaller block|He possibly thought that in the position I was holding I might have some ''voice'' in whatever decision was arrived at.
{{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXVI. 861.}}}}

'''6.''' One who speaks; a speaker.

<poem>A potent ''voice'' of parliament,
A pillar steadfast in the storm.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cxiii.}}

{{smaller block|This no doubt is one of the chief praises of Gray, as of other poets, that he is the ''voice'' of emotions common to all mankind.
{{right|''Lowell'', New Princeton Rev., I. 173.}}}}

'''7.''' Wish or admonition made known in any way; command; injunction.

{{smaller block|Ye would not be obedient unto the ''voice'' of the Lord your God.
{{right|Deut. viii. 20.}}}}

{{smaller block|He is dull of hearing who understands not the ''voice'' of God, unless it be clamorous in an express and a loud commandment.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 8.}}}} '''8†.''' That which is said; report; rumor; hence, reputation; fame.
{{smaller block|<poem>The common ''voice'', I see, is verified
Of thee.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., v. 3. 176.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I fear you wrong him;
He has the ''voice'' to be an honest Roman.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Philenzo’s dead already; . . .
The ''voice'' is, he is poison’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shirley'', Bird in a Cage, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Lord of Andover is to have £20,000 in lieu of his mastership of the Horse, besides being to be made an earl and a privy counsellor, as the ''voice'' goes.
{{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', I. 19.}}}}
'''9†.''' A word; a term; a vocable.   ''Udall.''—'''10.''' In ''phonetics'', sound uttered with resonance of the vocal cords, and not with a mere emission of breath; sonant utterance.—'''11.''' In ''gram.'', that form of the verb or body of inflections which shows the relation of the subject of the affirmation or predication to the action expressed by the verb. {{smaller|In Latin there are two voices, active and passive, having different endings throughout. In Greek and Sanskrit the voices are active and middle, certain forms, mostly middle, being used in a passive sense. In English, again, there is no distinction of voices; every verb is active, and a passive meaning belongs only to certain verb-phrases, made with help of an auxiliary: thus, ''he is praised'', ''we have been loved''.—'''Equal voices,''' in ''music''. See ''equal''.—'''In my voice†''', in my name.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Implore her, ''in my voice'', that she make friends
To the strict deputy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 2. 185.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Inner voice.''' See ''inner part'', under ''inner''.—'''In voice''', in a condition of vocal readiness for effective speaking or singing.—'''Mean voice.''' See ''mean''<sup>3</sup>.—'''Middle voice''', in ''music''. See ''middle part'', under ''middle''.—'''Veiled voice.''' See ''veil'', ''n.'', 7.—'''Voice of the silence''', intelligible words which some persons seem to themselves to hear in certain hypnotic states, as the clairaudient, and also in some cerebral disorders; an auditory hallucination.—'''With one voice''', unanimously.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Greekish heads, which ''with one voice''
Call Agamemnon head and general.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3. 221.}}}}

'''voice''' (vois), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''voiced'', ppr. ''voicing''.   [< ''voice'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To give utterance to; assert; proclaim; declare; announce; rumor; report.
{{smaller block|Rather assume thy right in silence . . . than ''voice'' it with claims and challenges. {{right|''Bacon'', Great Place (ed. 1887).}}}}
{{smaller block|Here is much lamentation for the King of Denmark, whose disaster is ''voiced'' by all to be exceeding great.
{{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', I. 148.}}}}
{{smaller block|We are, in fact, ''voicing'' a general and deepening discontent with the present state of society among the working classes. {{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLIII. 229.}}}}
'''2.''' To fit for producing the proper sounds; regulate the tone of: as, to ''voice'' the pipes of an organ. See ''voicing''.—'''3.''' To write the voice-parts of.   ''Hill'', Dict. Mus. Terms.—'''4†.''' To nominate; adjudge by acclamation; declare.
{{smaller block|<poem>Your minds,
Pre-occupied with what you rather must do
Than what you should, made you against the grain
To ''voice'' him consul.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3. 242.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Like the drunken priests
In Bacchus’ sacrifices, without reason
''Voicing'' the leader-on a demi-god.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Broken Heart, i. 2.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
